stories.title: Chicago/Midwest People & Company News, week of September 4, 2026
stories.excerpt: CBRE has promoted Chris Schastok to vice chairman, the firm’s highest professional title for producers. Schastok is a member of CBRE’s Site Selection & Incentives group within the Advisory Services Practice, based in Chicago. For more than 13 years at the firm, he has helped clients translate business objectives into site selection strategy and economic incentive negotiations, working alongside the broader planning and execution of corporate real estate initiatives. He has negotiated billions in incentives on clients’ behalf, with experience across corporate headquarters, food production, manufacturing and distribution center projects. Oxford Companies, a commercial real estate firm serving the greater Ann Arbor area, announced that Neal Warling has joined the company as director of sales and leasing. Warling will help lead Oxford’s brokerage activities, working with property owners, investors, tenants and corporate clients. The firm also announced the promotions of three longtime members of its leadership team, naming Joe Mifsud chief operating officer, Katie Vohwinkle senior vice president of operations, and Mike Van Patten senior vice president of asset management. PREMIER Design + Build Group announced that David Lewis has joined the company as general superintendent, based in its Columbus, Ohio, office. In his new role, Lewis will provide field leadership for the company’s Ohio operations, overseeing project execution while supporting operational excellence, safety, quality, and the continued development of field teams. Lewis brings more than four decades of construction experience, including more than 30 years in field management and leadership roles. CenterPoint Properties has appointed Ross Straseske as executive vice president and chief financial officer. bullets: CBRE promotes Chris Schastok to vice chairman; negotiated billions in incentives for corporate real estate.
Oxford Companies expands Ann Arbor leadership; Joe Mifsud named COO, Katie Vohwinkle SVP operations.
PREMIER Design + Build appoints David Lewis as general superintendent for Columbus, Ohio operations.
stories.summary: CBRE elevated Schastok, a Site Selection & Incentives specialist with 13+ years tenure and deep experience in corporate HQ and industrial incentive deals. Oxford Companies also promoted three senior leaders into newly formalized roles (COO, SVP Operations, SVP Asset Management), signaling organizational scaling in the Ann Arbor market. PREMIER Design + Build hired a 40-year construction veteran as general superintendent to lead Ohio field operations. These moves reflect regional consolidation and leadership depth in Midwest development and brokerage.
stories.impact: Not directly material to multifamily development demand or supply. These are primarily personnel moves in adjacent real estate services and construction trades; no signal of new residential demand drivers, capital availability changes, or cost shifts affecting apartment development underwriting.

stories.title: CEDARst Snags $80M Construction Loan for San Diego Apartments
stories.excerpt: CEDARst obtained an $80 million construction financing for The Samuel, a 197-unit Class A multifamily development in San Diego’s North Park neighborhood. JLL worked on behalf of the CEDARst Companies, in arranging the three-year, floating-rate loan through CrossHarbor Capital Partners. The Samuel will be located at 2821 Adams Ave. in North Park. The eight-story development will feature 82 studios, 93 one- and 22 two-bedroom units, averaging 621 square feet, with 189 parking spaces. The development will include amenities such as a pool, fitness center, co-working lounge, fire pits, game deck and a rooftop sunset lounge with an outdoor kitchen. Construction is expected to begin in Q3 2026, with completion anticipated in Q4 2028. JLL Capital Market’s Debt Advisory team was led by Senior Director Zach Kersten, Director Jack Wood and Analyst Ben Choromanski. bullets: CEDARst secures $80M floating-rate construction loan from CrossHarbor Capital for The Samuel, San Diego.
197-unit Class A development in North Park; 8-story, 621 SF avg, construction Q3 2026–Q4 2028.
JLL arranged three-year loan; amenities include pool, fitness, co-working, rooftop sunset lounge.
stories.summary: CEDARst obtained $80 million in construction financing via CrossHarbor Capital Partners for The Samuel, a 197-unit Class A multifamily project in San Diego's North Park neighborhood. The development is an eight-story, mixed-unit product (studios, 1BR, 2BR) averaging 621 square feet, with construction starting Q3 2026 and completion expected Q4 2028. JLL's debt advisory team led the financing arrangement on a three-year, floating-rate structure.
stories.impact: San Diego multifamily financing remains active and competitive; floating-rate construction debt is available for Class A new construction in supply-constrained, affluent submarkets like North Park. However, floating-rate exposure signals lender and sponsor confidence in near-term stabilization and rate environment—typical for 2026–2028 deliveries. North Park's tight supply and high barriers to entry support feasibility for premium-positioned new construction.

stories.title: Colliers Completes 67K-SF Industrial Lease in Maryland
stories.excerpt: Colliers completed a 67,040-square-foot industrial lease at 4780 Winchester Boulevard in Frederick, Maryland. Executive Vice Presidents Thomas Gentner, Brian Siegel and Jason Sullivan represented the landlord in the transaction. Link Logistics is an owner and operator of last-mile industrial real estate, with approximately 500 million square feet of warehouse space across 3,000 properties in North America. The new tenant, Senneca Holdings, Inc., is a manufacturer of data center containment solutions, specialty doors, and space separation systems. said Michael Walsh, Senior Vice President and Market Officer at Link Logistics. “We’re pleased to welcome Senneca Holdings and remain committed to providing properties that help our customers operate efficiently while meeting their evolving needs.” Located within one of the Mid-Atlantic’s most strategically positioned industrial corridors, 4780 Winchester Boulevard offers immediate access to Route 15, Interstate 70 and Interstate 270, providing connectivity to Washington, D.C., Baltimore, Northern Virginia and major East Coast population centers. The post Colliers Completes 67K-SF Industrial Lease in Maryland appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Link Logistics leases 67,040 SF industrial space in Frederick, Maryland to Senneca Holdings.
Senneca manufactures data center containment solutions, specialty doors, space separation systems.

stories.summary: Link Logistics completed a 67,040-square-foot industrial lease at 4780 Winchester Boulevard in Frederick, Maryland, with Senneca Holdings, a manufacturer of data center containment and specialty solutions. The property is strategically located within the Mid-Atlantic industrial corridor with immediate access to Routes 15, I-70, I-270, and connectivity to Washington, D.C., Baltimore, and Northern Virginia. Colliers represented the landlord on the transaction.
stories.impact: Marginal to multifamily. This signals data center adjacency and specialized manufacturing growth in the Frederick/Mid-Atlantic corridor, which could attract workforce in-migration and support apartment demand in DC suburbs over time. However, this is a single industrial lease; no direct bearing on near-term multifamily supply, financing, or development feasibility.

stories.title: New Details Released for Kent Manufacturing and Innovation Campus
stories.excerpt: Growing demand from aerospace, defense, space, and emerging technology companies is driving plans for the Kent Manufacturing & Innovation Campus (KMIC), a proposed 9.3-acre industrial development in the Pacific Northwest. Mortenson is advancing the project in partnership with the city of Kent. The 9.3-acre site is emerging as a future home for specialized occupiers seeking customized next-gen space in the Pacific Northwest. Marketed by Kidder Mathews, the KMIC campus can accommodate 150,000 to 300,000 square feet of customized manufacturing, research and development, office, and industrial space. The property benefits from proximity to a recently upgraded Puget Sound Energy substation capable of supporting up to 20 megawatts of power. “In nearly every conversation we’re having with advanced manufacturers, electrical capacity is a key topic as automation, robotics, and other advanced production technologies continue to drive demand,” said Kidder’s Matt Murray, SIOR, who leads leasing efforts alongside Chris Corr and Dane Dahline, SIOR. The project recently received SEPA approval, completing the project’s environmental review process. bullets: Kent Manufacturing & Innovation Campus (KMIC), 9.3 acres, Pacific Northwest; 150K–300K SF customizable space.
Mortenson + city of Kent partnership; aerospace, defense, space, emerging tech demand drivers.
Recently upgraded Puget Sound Energy substation supports 20 megawatts; SEPA environmental approval completed.
stories.summary: Mortenson is advancing the Kent Manufacturing & Innovation Campus, a 9.3-acre industrial development in Kent, Washington (Pacific Northwest), in partnership with the city. The project can accommodate 150,000–300,000 square feet of customized manufacturing, R&D, office, and industrial space targeting aerospace, defense, space, and emerging tech occupiers. The site benefits from a recently upgraded Puget Sound Energy substation capable of supporting 20 megawatts of power, and has received SEPA environmental approval.
stories.impact: Aerospace, defense, and advanced manufacturing cluster growth in Pacific Northwest (Puget Sound region near Seattle) signals strong local job and population in-migration tailwinds for multifamily. Specialized industrial development with elevated power capacity attracts high-skill, higher-wage occupiers. This supports apartment demand growth in Seattle metro and Kent submarket; developers should monitor tenant announcements and lease-up to forward-estimate workforce migration and household formation 12–24 months out.

stories.title: Joint Venture Picks Up 50-Building Silicon Valley R&D Portfolio
stories.excerpt: A joint venture of TMG Partners, Grove Real Estate Partners and an affiliate of Lone Star Real Estate Fund VII acquired a 2.2 million-square-foot portfolio of R&D assets spread across six campuses in Silicon Valley. Commercial Search reports that Washington Holdings sold the collection. With 50 buildings spanning 140 acres, it’s the largest institutionally owned portfolio of Class A, predominantly single-story, mission-critical research and development properties in Silicon Valley, according to the new owners. TMG Partners and Grove Real Estate Partners will operate the portfolio. The sale price was not disclosed. Washington Holdings invested approximately $173 million into base building, exterior and interior renovations across the portfolio during its ownership. The properties are located within a 5-mile radius of each other within the Golden Triangle in Santa Clara, San Jose and Milpitas, Calif. The portfolio is 87 percent leased to a roster of 63 tenants. The properties are: Zanker Place, Mission Park R&D, Montague Square, North First @ Orchard Station, and Montague Oaks. The post Joint Venture Picks Up 50-Building Silicon Valley R&D Portfolio appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: TMG Partners, Grove Real Estate Partners, Lone Star Fund VII acquire 50-building Silicon Valley R&D portfolio.
2.2M SF, 140 acres, 6 campuses (Golden Triangle: Santa Clara, San Jose, Milpitas); 87% leased to 63 tenants.
Class A, mission-critical single-story R&D; largest institutionally owned portfolio of type in Silicon Valley.
stories.summary: A joint venture of TMG Partners, Grove Real Estate Partners, and Lone Star Real Estate Fund VII acquired a 2.2 million-square-foot portfolio of 50 Class A, predominantly single-story R&D buildings across six campuses in Silicon Valley's Golden Triangle (Santa Clara, San Jose, Milpitas). The portfolio spans 140 acres, is 87 percent leased to 63 tenants, and is the largest institutionally owned collection of mission-critical R&D properties in the region. Sale price was undisclosed; Washington Holdings invested ~$173 million in renovations during its ownership.
stories.impact: Institutional capital remains deeply committed to Silicon Valley R&D and life sciences despite broader market uncertainty. 87% occupancy and institutional consolidation signal stable, long-term tech/life sciences employment and talent retention in the region. Multifamily developers in San Jose, Milpitas, and Santa Clara should expect sustained demand from knowledge workers anchored to these campuses; proximity to R&D clusters commands rent and rent-growth premiums. Monitor tenant stability and expansion signals to forecast headcount and household formation in adjacent residential markets.

stories.title: Reuben Brothers’ Jordana Yechiel On the Firm’s Big Bet on Century City
stories.excerpt: Century City has long been one of Los Angeles’ most concentrated office districts, but Reuben Brothers is betting that the area’s next chapter will look far more residential, experiential and luxury-driven. At Century Plaza, the development firm is building up around the Fairmont Century Plaza hotel and Park Elm condominiums, layering in restaurants, galleries, expansive wellness offerings and a revamped public plaza. For Jordana Yechiel (nee Reuben) of Reuben Brothers, the strategy reflects a larger shift in how people want to live in Los Angeles, drawing inspiration from Dubai’s International Financial Centre becoming a round-the-clock destination, where restaurants, culture and residences transformed what had largely been a business district. Commercial Observer spoke with Yechiel in late August about why Reuben Brothers made such a large bet on Century City, what luxury buyers expect, and how the firm is curating tenants rather than chasing occupancy and rent. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: Reuben Brothers has traditionally focused on trophy real estate and hospitality. What made Century City and this project fit the portfolio? Jordana Yechiel: At Reuben Brothers, the anomaly in our portfolio is Century City. We started as a traditional real estate company, and then we went into hospitality and luxury hotels and some residential development. But these were always trophy assets, whether they were in London, or the Surrey Hotel on the Upper East Side, or we’ve now made the Waldorf Astoria out of the W in South Beach. Real trophy property first, hospitality second. So we look at the property as a property deal, because that’s the way our brains are wired, and then we bring the luxury to it. This is a new development. We’ve poured more money into this than anything else. Our belief behind this was we don’t want to just put more stuff out into the world. We want to say, “What’s missing? What’s working? How can we help?
bullets: Reuben Brothers converting Century Plaza (Century City, Los Angeles) into mixed-use luxury destination.
Park Elm Residences condos + Fairmont Century Plaza hotel + restaurants, galleries, wellness, public plaza.
Strategy: residential, experiential, luxury-driven repositioning of former office-centric district.
stories.summary: Reuben Brothers is executing a large mixed-use redevelopment at Century Plaza in Century City, Los Angeles, anchored by the Fairmont Century Plaza hotel and Park Elm Residences condominiums, layered with restaurants, galleries, wellness facilities, and an upgraded public plaza. The firm's strategy reflects a shift toward residential and experiential uses in what was historically a concentrated office district, drawing inspiration from Dubai's International Financial Centre model of mixed-use 24/7 destinations.
stories.impact: Century City office-to-residential/mixed-use conversion signals broader adaptive reuse trend in Los Angeles submarkets with weak office fundamentals. Reuben's luxury-focused positioning and tenant curation (not occupancy chasing) indicate high-end residential demand remains resilient in L.A. Developers should monitor Century City's retail, hospitality, and residential lease-up metrics and pricing to validate luxury repositioning thesis and assess spillover demand into adjacent Century City multifamily submarkets. This is a canary for office conversion feasibility in high-barrier L.A. locations.

stories.title: Downtown D.C. Office Conversion Secures $176M Loan, New Majority Partner
stories.excerpt: One of Washington, D.C.’s largest office-to-residential redevelopments has secured a new majority partner and $175.6 million in construction financing. A partnership of Stonebridge, the Bernstein Companies and Criterion Real Estate Capital sold a 72 percent stake in the conversion of 1990 K Street NW to an entity managed by MetLife Investment Management for $58.7 million, according to records reported by the Business Journals. Kennedy Wilson Capital led the financing along with U.S. Fire Insurance, North River Insurance, Odyssey Reinsurance and Allied World Assurance. Cushman & Wakefield’s D.C.-based capital markets and debt advisory team arranged the financing. The roughly $250 million redevelopment, which will be rebranded as 1999 Eye Street NW, will replace the former office building with a 14-story, 412,000-square-foot mixed-use property. Plans call for 340 market-rate apartments, 44 affordable units, 50 student housing units totaling 200 beds, along with 15,600 square feet of retail and 189 parking spaces. Bernstein bought the property for $55.8 million in 2001, and Stonebridge and Criterion joined the ownership group last year. Demolition started in September 2025. The project is part of D.C.’s Housing in Downtown program, which offers a 20-year tax abatement for qualifying commercial-to-residential conversions and redevelopments. It is the second-largest project in the program’s pipeline, behind the planned conversion of the Universal Buildings on Connecticut Avenue into roughly 600 units. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: 1990 K Street NW (Washington, D.C.) office-to-residential conversion secures $175.6M construction financing + new partner.
MetLife Investment Management acquires 72% stake for $58.7M; Kennedy Wilson Capital leads debt.
412K SF mixed-use: 340 market-rate apartments, 44 affordable units, 50 student housing (200 beds), retail, parking.
stories.summary: A major office-to-residential conversion at 1990 K Street NW in Washington, D.C. (rebranding as 1999 Eye Street NW) secured $175.6 million in construction financing and a new majority partner. MetLife Investment Management acquired a 72 percent stake for $58.7 million, with Kennedy Wilson Capital leading the debt package. The ~$250 million redevelopment will create 412,000 square feet of mixed-use space: 340 market-rate apartments, 44 affordable units, 50 student housing units (200 beds), 15,600 SF of retail, and 189 parking spaces.
stories.impact: D.C. office conversion is now institutional-grade with long-term capital commitments; MetLife's majority investment signals confidence in downtown D.C. residential fundamentals and mixed-use absorption. Large affordable and student housing components indicate subsidy/demand tail-winds (likely powered by D.C. tax credits, inclusionary zoning mandates). Developers underwriting downtown D.C. multifamily and adaptive reuse should expect continued institutional capital availability and elevated development costs tied to mixed-use complexity and affordable units. This validates D.C. office conversion pipeline; monitor lease-up, rent achievement, and cap-rate compression to assess market absorption capacity.

stories.title: Geoff Mason Promoted to U.S. Chief Operating Officer of Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield
stories.excerpt: Retail operator Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield (URW) has elevated a longtime executive to the role of chief operating officer for its U.S. business. URW promoted Geoff Mason from vice president of asset management and development to COO after a series of successful development launches in Chicago, New Jersey and Southern California, according to the mall giant. Mason will be stepping into the shoes of Dominic Lowe, who will leave the company after 18 years, according to Westfield. “Geoff is an exceptional leader who brings a deep understanding of our U.S. portfolio, strong relationships across the organization and a clear vision for the future of our centers,” URW CEO Vincent Rouget said in a statement. Mason worked for URW from 2007 to 2016 before spending two and a half years at Macerich. He then returned to URW as senior vice president of operating management in 2018, according to Mason’s LinkedIn profile. “Over the past eight years, I have seen firsthand the strength of URW’s U.S. portfolio and the Westfield brand,” Mason said in a statement, adding that he plans to improve assets to serve as flagship locations for retailers. Mason assumed the role of COO on Sept. 1, according to Westfield. The appointment seems to strengthen the mall operator’s resolve to remain in the U.S. market despite plans announced in 2022 to focus on European assets. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield (URW) promotes Geoff Mason to U.S. Chief Operating Officer.
Mason succeeds Dominic Lowe after 18 years; led successful development launches in Chicago, New Jersey, Southern California.
URW prioritizing asset improvement and flagship retail positioning across U.S. portfolio.
stories.summary: Retail operator URW promoted Geoff Mason from VP of asset management and development to Chief Operating Officer of its U.S. business, replacing Dominic Lowe. Mason has led development launches in Chicago, New Jersey, and Southern California and brings deep portfolio expertise. URW's CEO emphasized Mason's vision for improving assets as flagship locations for retailers.
stories.impact: Not material to multifamily development. URW is a retail REIT; Mason's COO promotion signals URW's focus on mixed-use and experiential retail real estate, which may support adjacent multifamily opportunities in urban/lifestyle retail corridors (e.g., Westfield centers in major metros). However, no direct signal of demand, supply, financing, or cost drivers affecting apartment development.

stories.title: Sagehall Picks Up Chetrit Organization’s 428 Broadway for $47M
stories.excerpt: An entity linked to New York City-based private real estate investment firm Sagehall has purchased Chetrit Organization’s office building at 428 Broadway for $47 million, according to city records filed Thursday. Jason Levine, managing director at Sagehall, signed for the buyer entity, 428 Broadway Owner. The seller entities are a partnership between the Chetrit Organization, for which Michael Chetrit signed on behalf of two holding companies, and investor American Industrial, co-founded by Roget Lerner and Jean-Marc Donics, the latter of whom signed on behalf of entity AI SoHo Investors. Chetrit Group purchased the six-story property in Manhattan’s SoHo neighborhood in 2005 for $22.5 million. It became the property of the Chetrit Organization in the years following the family’s enterprise split in the mid-2000s. The building eventually ran into distress after its four-floor anchor tenant, WeWork, filed for bankruptcy in 2023. The coworking firm’s departure from 428 Broadway left the building 96 percent vacant. Its current level of occupancy is unclear. Lender LoanCore Capital Credit began foreclosure actions against 428 Broadway in 2024, alongside 1 Whitehall Street in the Financial District, claiming default on roughly $200 million worth of loans. The latter office building was sold earlier this year for $105 million to Nathan Berman’s Metro Loft and Idan Ofer’s Quantum Pacific Group for a planned residential conversion. The mortgage debt on 428 Broadway appears to have changed hands from LoanCore to an entity belonging to Chetrit Organization and Donics, C&AI Soho Holding, in late 2025. The entity took ownership of the property in a recent foreclosure auction, allowing the partners to facilitate a sale. Donic declined to comment on the recent sale, while spokespeople for Sagehall and Chetrit did not immediately respond to requests for comment. bullets: Sagehall acquires Chetrit Organization's 428 Broadway (Manhattan SoHo) office building for $47M.

stories.summary: Sagehall purchased the Chetrit Organization's six-story office building at 428 Broadway in Manhattan's SoHo neighborhood for $47 million. The property became severely distressed after its four-floor anchor tenant, WeWork, filed for bankruptcy in 2023, leaving the building 96 percent vacant. Chetrit had acquired the property in 2005 for $22.5 million; the 2026 sale at $47 million reflects a distressed exit by the ownership partnership.
stories.impact: SoHo office is structurally weak; major tenant bankruptcies (WeWork) and high vacancy indicate limited hope for traditional office recovery. Sagehall's acquisition at distressed pricing may signal conversion intent (office-to-residential/creative/hospitality). Developers should monitor whether Sagehall pursues adaptive reuse or hold-for-conversion in SoHo. If 428 Broadway converts to multifamily, it signals opportunity cost for traditional office and potential repositioning of SoHo toward residential/lifestyle uses. However, SoHo's condominium-heavy market and strict NYC zoning may limit conversion upside; watch for signals of intent.

stories.title: Rockpoint Buys Oceanfront Fort Lauderdale Hotel for $47M
stories.excerpt: Rockpoint and Newbond Holdings have paid $47.1 million for an oceanfront resort in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., property records show. Called Hotel Maren Fort Lauderdale Beach, the property features 141 rooms at 525 South Fort Lauderdale Beach Boulevard, adjacent to Seebreeze Boulevard, south of Las Olas Boulevard. Magna Hospitality Group sold the 245,081-square-foot hotel, which is part of Hilton’s Curio Collection. “Hotel Maren is a high-quality beachfront property in a compelling submarket with attractive long-term fundamentals,” Patrick Ryan, a managing director at Rockpoint, said in a statement. “We believe there is a meaningful opportunity to build on the hotel’s existing strengths through targeted enhancements of the property and guest experience.” Apollo Global Management’s Athene Annuity & Life Assurance Company supplied a $47.7 million acquisition loan. A public deed listed the purchase price as $47.1 million, which likely valued only the hotel’s real estate. The final transaction value is probably higher to factor in the hotel’s business operations. A representative for Rockpoint declined to comment. The seller, Magna Hospitality, purchased the hotel out of bankruptcy mid-construction in 2018, paying $39.1 million, The Real Deal reported. Three years later, the Rhode Island-based hospitality company completed the 12-story building on a 0.7-acre site. The Rockpoint sale comes less than a month after El-Ad National Properties paid $60 million for another oceanfront hotel in Fort Lauderdale: the 1.2-acre, 99-room Sea Club Resort. Rockpoint, a private equity firm, has long been a major player in South Florida real estate. This year, the Boston-based firm has nabbed two construction loans each worth more than $100 million to build multifamily projects in Boca Raton and Palm Beach Gardens. bullets: Rockpoint + Newbond Holdings purchase Hotel Maren Fort Lauderdale (141 rooms) for $47.1M.

stories.summary: Rockpoint and Newbond Holdings acquired Hotel Maren Fort Lauderdale Beach, a 141-room oceanfront Hilton Curio Collection property at 525 South Fort Lauderdale Beach Boulevard, for $47.1 million. Magna Hospitality Group was the seller. Apollo Global Management's Athene Annuity & Life Assurance supplied a $47.7 million acquisition loan. Rockpoint plans targeted enhancements to guest experience and property positioning.
stories.impact: Hospitality investment in Fort Lauderdale beach corridor is not a direct multifamily signal, but oceanfront hospitality acquisitions by institutional sponsors suggest strong South Florida tourism/leisure fundamentals and visitor economy growth. This may drive ancillary support services and seasonal workforce, but does not materially affect apartment demand drivers (permanent resident base, employment) or supply/capital/cost factors. Minimal impact to multifamily development.
